HEADLINE: Other Passions
TEXT:
YASMINE GHONI EM Founder, co-director of interior design studioYSG Age: 40 Lives: Sydney

Yougrewup inKuwait,Saudi Arabia andEgypt.

Howdidthat influenceyour lifenowas founder of yourown interior design studio?

I attended international schools and consider my upbringing to have been rather liberating because of all the exposure I had to different cultures, religions and values.

I danced since I was four and was in and out of various bands for years. I started a band with a school girlfriend whose penthouse I’m currently designing in Kuwait.My fatherwas keen forme to pursue a career thatwould secure financial stability.

In Sydney, youwere singer-songwriter in a band calledTheConversations for sevenyears.How did theswitchtoLatindancingcomeup?

In our 30s everyonewas having babies and it became hard to keep the band together. I didn’t know much about Latin dancing until I joined LatinDance Australia about a year ago, and it has truly changedmy everyday. I started taking randomclasses in bachata, Brazilian salsa and samba, and fell in love with samba. I’ve been having private lessons and just got admitted into theMV Samba Elite Team.

Congratulations! That sounds prestigious.

It’s really a passport to performing.Hard work, practice and dedication will get you there. Prestigious – maybe not. Flipping awesome – hell yes! Describe the sambaoutfit andhow long is a typical dance?

Lots of sequins, strappy gold heels and feather headsets; think peacock vibes.My teacher,Debralee Scarselletta, is a threetimes world champion; she designs and makes all the costumes herself. Performance length is three to four minutes tops, but the exertion to pull off the three to four minutes is huge. It’s kind of like thewhole humanversus- dog-year thing.

You’rewearingDoc Martens today. I’mguessing you’re not a regular high-heelswearer?

No, so it’s pretty intense. Heels change the way youmove. My first performance is in September, so I’ve got some time to practise.

What aboutmanaging thewardrobe?

It’s tricky because of your headpiece.

Imagine placing something on your head and it staying quiet, then just letting everything below the neck go wild.

It sounds quite different to your ballet training.

Itwas quite frustrating in fact, because ballet’s very strict and rigid and samba is totally the opposite.You have to retrain and rethink how you use your body.

Doyouhaveadancepartner?

I was doing partnerwork but I just wanted to dance and not have to think about another person. Samba lets you do that.

Lessons are like a recharge button. I arrive solo, dance solo and get into my groove.

You’re planning to launch your own furniture line at theendof the year – impressivegiven YSG is only eight yearsold.

We’re working on a couple of different pieces that can sit together, that hark from my heritage, and provide some space-saving.

I love clever design. It’s got to be really functional but it’s amazing if it looks good too.And it will be made in Australia.

Describe your design style and your approach.

My end goal is always about evoking feelings rather than a fixed visual conclusion, so spending time onmy own in a space prior to any presentation to a client is fundamental. I guess I’m a choreographer of sorts because space occupies my mind as much as furnishings and fixtures. I think about movement within it – areas to pause, key access points, heavy traffic areas and journeys fromone zone to another.

Are younervous aboutbeingon stagesoon?

We’re on stage every day, aren’t we?

Whether it’s presenting a concept to a client, singing to a crowd, or performing a three-minute routine to strangers, it’s all about connectivity to the human spirit. I givemy all to everything I do. But I can live off a performance high for days, there’s nothing quite like it. •

HEADLINE: The high life
TEXT:
How to drink in a design-led European cocktail bar,without a passport.

On the 22nd level of Sydney’s A By Adina hotel, the darkly dramatic venue was devised by interior architect George Livissianis with classic cocktail bar glamour in mind. Booths are black leather, the piano is a baby grand, and fine-stemmed coupettes perch on gold-veined marble tables like wild, fragile birds.

Trained in the dark arts of bartending in Europe’s finest hotel bars, owners Andrea Gualdi, Stefano Catino and MartinHudak know that a great cocktail ismore than the sumof its parts. It’swhy their first bar, Maybe Sammy in The Rocks, won the 2019 global MichterArt of Hospitality Award before it was 12months old.Now they have taken the idea of a cocktail bar to new heights. Literally.

A sense of playfulness is built into drinks such asRolling ADouble,which comeswith a pair of dice.Roll a double and get a champagne upgrade. Likewise, Coffee Champagne arriveswith a little pot of fragrant hand cream, so that every time you lift the glass to your lips, you are enveloped in the dusky scent of coffee.

Acclaimed chef Jane Strode (ex-Bistrode) has created a menuwith a hotel bar attitude: crayfish club sandwiches, chicken liver parfait and tiramisu profiteroles.

JANE STRODE’S OYSTERS WITH NAM JIM AND A DRY MARTINI “This sweet, salty, limey dressing is best made just before serving,” says Jane Strode. “It’s also greatwith fried eggs, grilled ocean trout or a greenmango salad.”

INGREDIENTS • Freshly shucked Sydney rock oysters • 3 kaffir lime leaves • 4 coriander roots and stem, cleaned of any dirt • ½ long green chilli • 1 tbsp seeded mustard • 1 small finger of turmeric, peeled • 2 tbsp palm sugar • 6-8 tbsp lime juice • 1 to 2 tbsp fish sauce • 1/3 cup loosely packed Thai basil leaves • ½ teaspoon white pepper • 1 punnet micro coriander, tops trimmed with scissors METHOD Using a stick or bar blender, blend all the ingredients (except oysters andmicro coriander) to a smoothdressing.Check that the dressing tastes sweet, salty and sour,with a hint of heat, and adjust accordingly with palm sugar, fish sauce,white pepper and lime juice. Spoon over the oysters and topwith sprigs of coriander.

HOW TO MAKE A DRY MARTINI For Andrea Gualdi, there are two rules to the perfectmartini.

One, itmust be served very cold. Andtwo, thedilution (bartender speak for howthe ice reacts in theglass from beginning toend)must be meticulously controlled. The glass is almost an ingredient in itself, and should be chilled in the freezer before use. “The right glass will help recreate that classic cocktail experience,” says Gualdi. “I really like a tiny coupette [small, stemmed cocktail glass], so you get a wider brim that will give youway more aroma.”

Athome, he useswhatever Australianginor vodkahe finds interesting at themoment, while for the vermouth, he favours ItalianbrandOscar.697.

“It’s a very gooddry vermouth, with almost a touch of salinity to it. But if Iwanted something easy tofind, itwouldhave tobe Noilly Prat.”

As for the ratio: “Iusually go for 60ml of ginor vodka, and 10 to 15ml of vermouth.” For a “wetter”martini, Gualdi will use up to 20ml of vermouth.

He starts by adding ice to the glass. “Stir the ice tocool the glass, then discard the ice and thewater.”Water is the enemy of a perfect drymartini.

Pour themeasure of gin or vodka directly overmore ice in amixing jug, stir onceor twice, then strain into the glass until almost full.

Gualdi’s pro tip? Add both an olive anda twistof lemon zest to the finished martini, then discard the zest, leaving just the traceof its aroma. “The martini is extremely simple,” he says, “but it is oneof the hardest drinks toget right.”•

HEADLINE: Brandy snaps back
TEXT:
Distillers are taking advantage of a burst in popularity for dark spirits

At the time, co-founder Bob Laing told me this was because Australian brandy suffered from a terrible image problem. Too many people, he said, thought of brandy as cheap, low-quality and old-fashioned.

Now things are different, there’s a thirst for premiumproducts andmuchmore knowledge. So, I’ve changed the description of what we make to ‘fine aged brandies’. I reallywant to play a strong role in revitalising the image of brandy and celebrating the incredible history of quality brandy production in this country.”

Richard Angove is the fifth-generation member of the South Australian family behind StAgnes brandy, due to celebrate its centenary in 2025, and he is also determined to revive the drink’s image.

He says thatwhile sales of the St Agnes brandies at the cheaper end of the price spectrum cater for “the mature market”, the brandies at the super-premium end – culminating in the 40-year-old Imperial XO, which sells for $750 a bottle – have been discovered by a new generation of craft spirits consumerswho arewilling to spend goodmoney for fine drinks.

“We’ve really seen an uptick in sales of the XOs in the last three years,” says Angove. “We’re partly riding on the coat tails of single malt whisky, I think. People have become seriously interested in top-quality dark spirits of all kinds.”

The quality is undeniable. Earlier this year, a single-cask XO brandy from Tasmanian distillery Sullivans Cove took out the top trophy at theWorld Brandy Awards. And at last year’s Australian Distilled SpiritsAwards, although the number of brandies entered was dwarfed by the flood of other dark spirits entered, the brandies won twice as many gold medals as either the whiskies or the rums.

The next stage in brandy’s development in Australia, says Angove, is in themiddle ground: spirits that sit somewhere between the cheap-and-cheerful supermarket brands and the expensive bottles aimed at collectors. Angove’s first entry into this market is Bartender’s Cut, an $80 brandy developed in conjunction with Seb Costello, owner of all-Australian spirits bar Bad Frankie, and other hospitality professionals.

“We got everyone together at Bad Frankie to do a blending session,” saysAngove. “It got us out of our comfort zone. Here were the people who sell brandy in their bars telling us what they wanted to see – which was an unashamedly Australian brandy, rich and full of the flavour of the tawny port and sherry barrels used to age the spirit.”

BARTENDER’S CUT BRANDY RIVERLAND $80 With a higher-than-normal alcohol content of 44per cent, this is a bold and beautiful brandy: enticing, complex aromas of grape spirit and spice, and a lovely, lingering ginger-snap sweetness.

stagnesdistillery.com.au ST AGNES XO 15 YEAR OLD BRANDY RIVERLAND $114 Three-time winner of the best brandy trophy at the Australian Distilled Spirits Awards, this is fabulously multi-layered and deeply satisfying, withrichflavours of Sevillemarmalade and a super-silky texture.

HEADLINE: Hut Destination
TEXT:
Wilga Stationmight evoke the era ofwhen the nation rode on the sheep’s back, but these days it’s after couples and ‘girls getaways’ rather than sweaty shearers

INTHEEARLY 2000S,WHENTHE “FREE and independent traveller” market was growing amongmiddle- to upper-class Asians, a curious category emerged: young women travellers who had the freedom and wherewithal to venture overseas alone; often in possession of their parents’ black Amex card, if not a chaperone.

Given their high-yielding spend in the countries they visited, the “solo saris” (as they became known out of India) quickly became a valuedmarket for high-end tourismoperators, fromManhattan to the Mornington Peninsula.

Wilga Station’s Farmers Hut opened earlier this year. The sheep farmis near Bathurst, about three hours’ drive from Sydney. Owner and third-generation farmer HamishKeith confesses he and wifeMez are in hot pursuit of these so-called “women packs”. “We’ve nailed theVolkswagen and Audi set for the FarmersHut,which is a secluded couple’s retreat – nowwe’re chasing thewomen packs for the fivebedroom Shearers Hall,” Keith explains.

We’re standing outside the Shearers Hall, built early last century on the 105-hectare working sheep property. It opens for guests in September, once a complete renovation of the heritage building is finished.

The definition of “women packs”, should you need one, is women aged from25 to 80 who enjoy travelling with female friends.

They come in the formof book clubs, professional groups, hens’ parties, or any other formof collaboration. “They tend to be cultured, independent, and appreciative of the finer things in life,” Keith says, before adding diplomatically that the Shearers Hall will also be available to mixed-gender or men’s groups and, of course, to families.

The Keiths bought out the family farm in 2018 after returning from a stint inNew York whereMez worked for the United Nations, and Hamish was in events management. Nowwith two small children, they’ve spent the past fewyears gentrifying this glorious plot of land, which features slabs of granite rock strewn around like naturally occurring sculptures, rustic remnants of the station’s glory years (sheep drenching pens, cattle yards), and swimming holes in the creek surrounded by basket willow trees and stately river gums.

But the real hero is theWilga sheep trail, a two-kilometrewinding track, carved out by decades of small determined hooves, that leads from the Farmers Hut to the creek.

“We spent thousands of dollars constructing a gorgeous eco hut,making it really beautiful, and if you read the guest book, the biggest fuss is over the sheep trail.

They love the accommodation, but they really love the sheep trail,” Keith says.

The open-plan Farmers Hut has a large bedroomand sitting areawith a showcase window; a small, efficient kitchen (with a covered barbecue area and fire pit just beyond the back door) and a modern bathroom. After settingmyself up, I stoke the wood burner stove Keith got going before my arrival, then join him for a property tour.

Bumping over the paddocks in his ute, he explains that guests can opt out of this tour; the genesis ofWilga is a true rural getaway whereby you can have a contactless experience if serious seclusion is your thing.

That’sWilga’s point of difference from other upmarket working sheep station-style Fiona Carruthers TRAVEL stays inNSW, such as Goonoo Goonoo near Tamworth or Callubri Station at Buddabadah, north-west of Dubbo. Guests can have the freedom, privacy and anonymity associated with an Airbnb, but also enjoy those nice little hotel touches – such as a hotline to “concierge”, fresh dinner packs delivered to your door to barbecue, and an antipasto board on arrival. If you do need them,Hamish and Mez are only 10minutes away in Bathurst.

Sitting by the fire that night in the Farmers Hut (I’d describe it more as a villa), savouring local goat’s cheese and olives, I muse thatWilga caters to a wonderfully underdevelopedmarket, whereby you get to live on a working property that also happens to be postcard perfect. The location really comes into its own when I step outside into the cold night to admire the full moon and am greeted by the gentle baa-ing of far-off sheep and their sprightly, May-born lambs. It’s just me, and about 500 of them.

Consider it your own little slice of #farmlyfe whereby you can spend a couple of days playing out squattocracy fantasies or maybe dissecting My Brilliant Career for book club (botanicals gin from just down the road to hand) – then drive off in a cloud of dust before sheep prices crash and a five-year drought sets in.

ThewriterwasaguestofWilga Station.

THE PLACE Wilga Station is at 1611 MidWestern Highway, Evans Plains,NSW. Email info@wilgastation.

com.auor tel 0427 688542.

THE RATES The FarmersHut is priced from$450 a night (sleeps two); from$1100 for the ShearersHall, which sleeps up to 10people in fivebedrooms, withone large livingarea. Includes a bottleof sparklingwhite and cheese/antipastoplatteron arrival.Minimum two-night stay applies.

HEADLINE: Jean Genesis
TEXT:
RECENTLY, A RUMOUR BEGAN on the fashion-political circuit (a Venn diagramwithmore overlap than you might imagine). North Korean leaderKim Jong-un had banned the wearing of skinny jeans.

The rumour, published by the likes of the BBC and The SouthChinaMorning Post, was debunked by Seoul-based New York Times writer Choe Sang-Hun, who found that although Jong-un frequently disavows the influence of capitalist-style clothing, jeans, skinny or not, were still allowed above the 38th parallel.

That the rumour spread with such ease saysmuch about its plausibility, which says asmuch, in turn, about North Korea’s strictures as it does about denim itself. Because denim has been controversial since its inception.

Though you probably associate denim best with America, it was in fact born in Nimes, France, where it gets its name (“serge de Nimes,” truncated over time).

There, it was popular with field workers who praised its durability, but the indigo used to dye it was banned in parts of the continent wherewoad, an inferior substitute, was grown under subsidy.The Germans even called indigo “devil’s dye.”

Ironically, indigo would later become one of themost valuable crops in the American south, harvested by African- American slaves, wearing ... denim. The fabric was a way of physically separating the slave class from land owners,who wore lace, linen and silk.

During the civil rightsmovements of the 1950s and 60s, denimwas reclaimed by activists, and wearing blue jeans and overalls became symbolic of the fight for equality for African-Americans. Wearing the uniformof slavery was a powerful message to society that it had not changed nearly enough. Soon itwas co-opted by Hollywood (to quote Madonna: Marlon Brando, Jimmy Dean) and hippie counter-culture figures like Abbie Hoffman.

But some in the civil rights movement avoided denimaltogether due to its connection with slavery. Singer James Brown refused towear denimand forbade his bandmembers fromdoing so.

It is startling to imagine that one kind of fabric can have such a rich and impactful history. Denim, so ubiquitous it is almost invisible, tells many stories: to some itmeans freedom(like the 1960s feminists whowore jeans as an expression of gender equality); to others, exploitation (like the Lesotho garment workers revealed last year to exchange sexual favours for work at denim factories used by some of theworld’s leading luxury brands).

Denim can mean opportunity, the way Australian company Outland is creating sustainable jeans by training Cambodian women, and therefore keeping them out of human trafficking.

It canmean environmental disaster – one pair of jeans usesmore than 3700 litres ofwater in its production alone – or a chance to do better, the way Levi’s is encouraging consumers to hold onto their old jeans by offering free repairs and alterations.

It can mean mobility, as in Tommy Hilfiger’s adaptable range of denim for differently-abled bodies. It can mean creativity, like when Calvin Klein debuted denimon the runway for the first time in 1976. It can symbolise a newworld, like for the East Berliners whowould await shipments fromLevi’s in 1978.

Denim is sexy (Brooke Shields), it is hard-working (Rosie the Riveter), it is cringey (Obama’s dad jeans). It can be quotidian, it can be haute couture. It has been used in legal proceedings (the “skinny jeans” defense) and it has become a pop culture joke (the Canadian tuxedo).

It is the envy of designers (Yves Saint Laurent told New York magazine he wished he’d invented blue jeans). It is worn by everyone from prisoners to presidents (andmaybe even former presidents who will become prisoners).

It is both inherently political and deeply superficial. Simply by glancing at its cut, waistline, hemlength and colour, you can tell somuch about itswearer. It says somuch, without even somuch as a label. You could be wearing it right now, in fact. Even inNorthKorea. •

“Exploringthe Fornasetti archives hadthe excitement of an archaeological dig,” he says. Fornasetti’s drawn statues appear across velvet dresses and shiny tops; its architectural drawings and visages featureon a rangeof bags. louisvuitton.com

HEADLINE: Youre not going out in that
TEXT: SNAKES ALIVE, COULD THIS r timepiece really be from that wellknown house of enviable accoutrements, Louis Vuitton? A Carpe Diem version of the Tambour, it tells the time on demand, without hands but with a presentation unlike any other. By pressing a reptileshaped push-piece on the right of the case, a snake’s head lifts to reveal an hour aperture positioned in the centre of a skull, while its tail oscillates towards adjacent minute markings. Signature monogram flowers appear in lieu of an eye and – yes, there’s more – the skull’s jaw emits a mocking laugh from which emerge the words “Carpe diem (seize the day)”. The complications required to achieve this – a jumping hour, retrograde minute, power reserve display and associated mechanisms (426 parts) – move in a “bafflingly harmonious way” we’re told, while readability, we’re assured, “is peerless”. No word on cost, but the Carpe Diem was two years in development and patents have been applied for. •

HEADLINE: Higher ground
TEXT:
TIMEPIECES THAT SHINE AS A STAGE FOR ARTS, CRAFTS AND UNABASHED SPLENDOUR.

PANTHER POWER

“WHO NEEDS A WATCH WHEN you have a phone” might be one of the most common comments watch lovers encounter, but it misses a vital point: watches don’t merely tell the time, they transfer a little joy to the wearer who’s so inclined.

In the case of high-end and jewellery watches, they can bring even deeper enjoyment, along with the visual impact and delight of a sparkling adornment.

That’s something, obviously, that no phone has achieved, a fact seemingly not lost at a time of increased personal wealth and spending power.

Forbes reports that despite the pandemic, the rich have become even richer, the number of billionaires among us ballooning.

Which might go some way to explaining the proliferation of watches that cater not so much to day-to-day demands as to our dreams – and the dreams of those creating them.

Cartier, not unnaturally, is one of those leading the charge, bringing its “house” pet, the panther, to life in a fresh way, declaring: “It isn’t about imitating or exactly reproducing the animal, instead it’s about offff ering a new take on the richness of this source of inspiration.”

As Cartier’s director of design for watchmaking, Marie-Laure Cérède, explained to Watch: “Our commitment to Cartier is to get inspired by the archives, but also to transparent blue enamel revealing the underlyingdecoration, a rare handcrafts technique known as flinque enamel. The bezel gets a double rowof168TopWesseltonPure diamonds (~0.78carat) set using a Flamme technique. Inside, a self-windingmovement withtwo gongs for chiming the time keeps things suitably on song.

ON A WING Which brings us to Jaquet Droz,which in similar vein has produced the Bird Repeater, a lush automatonwith a minute repeater featuring multiple bird animations, eggs hatching and a flowing river all engraved and painted by hand.

Framed by a 47mm red gold case, two animated and vocal robins replicate “those that can be seen and heard all around the Swiss valleys”,while in the background is a replica of the farmhousewhere Pierre Jaquet-Droz was born 300 years ago.

This historical nod is couched in a verdant settingwith red berries and holly leaves, a blue butterfly – announcing the arrival of summer – a dragonfly and other animals.Never mind the time; here’s a watch to transport you to an idyllic Swiss location at the press of a button. EQUESTRIAN INSPIRATION For Hermès it’s not a bird, but a horse with wings inspiring the d’Hermès La Source de Pégase watch. Based on a silk scarf by French artist Pierre Marie, the dial depicts the mythological winged horse striking a rock with its hoof to create the Hippocrene spring on Mount Helicon.

SKY THE LIMIT Positioning itself as “the Roman jeweller of time”, Bulgari pulls no punches when it comes to its 2021 high-end collection, describing it as a “commitment to the value of magnificence” where “beauty, craftsmanship and inspiration converge into extraordinary works of art”.

If you’re wondering what kind of timepiece this might produce, look no further. The Celestial Sky watch is a oneoff that recalls the signature hues of the Roman sky, with an oval-shaped 6 carats Sri Lanka sapphire taking centre stage as a cover for a concealed pave dial.

Cast in platinum, the piece is a brazen bracelet of curved lines and bold volumes, “evoking the sinuosity of Baroque motifs” with 103 blue buff-top sapphires (11.44 carats), 10 tourmaline beads (27.9 carats), and 779 round brilliant-cut diamonds (20.9 carats) playing their part.

It comes with a quartz movement, which in a watch like this is a bonus rather than a drawback; it means no fiddly winding or resetting after sitting idle in the safe – where surely it’s going to spend most of its time. •
